newsitem.title: MEXICO: Rights groups allege abuses by Mexican army.
newsitem.headline: Rights groups allege abuses by Mexican army.

text.p: Mexican human rights groups accused the army on Monday of unleashing a wave of torture and repression in its hunt for leftist guerrillas in the western state of Guerrero.

Seven independent rights groups said they had documented cases of torture, kidnapping, disappearances and illegal searches of homes in the days after recent clashes in Guerrero between the army and Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) guerrillas. The battles killed at least nine people.

Rights groups said they feared the crackdown was in part politically motivated ahead of midterm elections on July 6, when Mexicans will vote for a new lower house of Congress, a third of the senate, six state governors and Mexico City's mayor.

"The aim of this military aggression only a month before federal elections is clear: to inhibit citizen participation in areas where the opposition is strong," a document signed by the seven groups said.
Recent polls have shown that Mexico's long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party could lose an unprecendented number of congressional seats in the race.

Seven members of Mexico's main leftist party were arrested and tortured by the army a day after EPR rebels and troops fought in the central part of the state last week, Lilia Moreno, head of human rights for the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), said.
After holding the men for a week without formal charges, the army released six of them over the weekend, Moreno said. One is still in prison on weapons charges.

Mexico's La Jornada newspaper on Monday carried interviews with the men, who said the army had arrested, blindfolded and tortured them for two days to force them to admit they belonged to or supported the Marxist rebel group.
The men were stripped naked, beaten and had water forced up their noses, they told La Jornada and the rights groups.
"In some cases, they were submitted to fake executions," the rights groups' document said.

Aurora Munoz, head of the Guerrero Institute for Human Rights, said impoverished peasant communities in Guerrero's remote mountains are virtually under a "state of siege" by army troops, which have carried out illegal searches of people and homes and blocked all roads in and out of the area.
Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo has vowed to crush the EPR, which first appeared in Guerrero in 1996, but has said the army will not resort to repression.

The battles in Guerrero were the first so far this year between the army and rebels, who said they were focusing on peaceful acts of "armed propaganda" to build support and had been encircled by advancing troops.
